chunks: What the Sheikh — may Allah the Exalted support him — informed me of, from Abu al-Qasim Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from 'Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn al-Mughira, from Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him), who said:
I asked: 'Is there a limit for istinja'?' He replied: 'No — until what is there is clean.'
I said: 'What if what is there is clean but the odor remains?' He said: 'The odor is not taken into consideration.'
Then he said: 'And he concludes by washing the outlet of urine from his penis.'
And what points to this [ruling is as follows]…

key_terms.الرِّيحُ: odor/smell — residual scent remaining after physical cleansing; ruled legally irrelevant to the validity of istinja'
key_terms.اَلِاسْتِنْجَاءُ: istinja' — ritual cleansing of the private parts after urination or defecation; a prerequisite component of tahara
key_terms.حَدٌّ: limit/threshold — a prescribed jurisprudential measure; here its absence means the criterion is qualitative (cleanliness), not quantitative
key_terms.مَخْرَجِ الْبَوْلِ: urethral outlet — the opening from which urine exits; washing it is the concluding act of istinja' for males

ai.seo_question: According to Shia hadith, is there a fixed limit for istinja', and does a lingering odor after physical cleanliness affect the validity of ritual purification?
ai.summary: This hadith records a jurisprudential ruling from Abu al-Hasan (AS) on the correct performance of istinja' (ritual cleansing of the private parts after answering the call of nature). The Imam establishes that there is no fixed numerical threshold — cleansing continues until the area is physically free of impurity — and that residual odor after physical cleanliness is legally disregarded. He further specifies that a male concludes the istinja' procedure by washing the urethral outlet.
